plan: Complete enhanced-ACT natural-science passage (CLD-P-ACT-R-000039, 'The Frog That Freezes'), about 560 words, on wood-frog freeze tolerance (extracellular ice, glucose and urea, Alaskan vs southern populations, organ-preservation interest). Topic checked against every verbal bank passage (no frog-freezing passage). 9 questions; claims hedged where figures vary by study.

passages.title: The Frog That Freezes
passages.text:
In the forests of North America, a small brown frog spends the winter in a state that looks, by every ordinary sign, like death. Buried under a few inches of leaf litter, the wood frog freezes. Its heart stops beating, its lungs stop moving, and much of the water in its body turns to ice. In spring, it thaws, its heart starts again, and within a day or so it is hopping toward a pond to breed. The frog is not the only animal that survives being frozen, but it is among the best studied.

Freezing kills most animals not because cold itself is harmful but because of what ice does to cells. When water inside a cell freezes, the growing crystals can tear the cell's membrane apart, and the damage cannot be undone when the ice melts. Ice that forms between cells, by contrast, does relatively little harm. The wood frog survives by controlling where the ice forms. Ice builds up in the spaces between its cells and in its body cavity, while the water inside the cells mostly stays liquid. As ice forms outside them, the cells lose water and shrink, and the fluid left inside becomes more concentrated and harder to freeze.

That shrinking would be dangerous on its own, since a cell that loses too much water can be damaged as well. Here the frog's second defense comes in. Within minutes after ice first touches its skin, the frog's liver begins converting a stored carbohydrate called glycogen into the sugar glucose and releasing it into the blood. Over the next several hours, glucose levels rise to many times their normal level, high enough to be deadly to a human. The sugar moves into the cells, where it holds on to water and limits how far the cells shrink. The frog also builds up a waste product called urea, which appears to help in a similar way.

Not all wood frogs can survive the same degree of cold. Frogs from populations in the southern part of the range survive only a few degrees below freezing. Frogs studied in Alaska, by contrast, have survived much lower temperatures in some studies. Researchers found that the Alaskan frogs entered winter with far larger stores of glycogen in their livers, and that they accumulated more urea during the fall. In the far north, where temperatures can stay well below freezing for months, that difference may decide which frogs live to breed in spring.

Biologists are interested in the wood frog for more than its own sake. Human organs donated for transplant can be kept outside the body for only a matter of hours, partly because they cannot be safely frozen. If tissue could be cooled below freezing without damage, organs might be stored for days or weeks instead. A frog that freezes and thaws every year without harm has been treated as a natural model for how living tissue might one day be preserved, though no one yet knows how far the frog's methods can be copied.

candidates.stem: Which of the following statements best expresses the main idea of the passage?

choices.A: Wood frogs avoid freezing by burying themselves deep beneath the forest floor.
choices.B: Wood frogs survive freezing by controlling where ice forms and by protecting their cells.
choices.C: Wood frogs have already shown doctors how to freeze human organs safely.
choices.D: Wood frogs from Alaska and from the south use completely different methods.

candidates.evidence: The wood frog survives by controlling where the ice forms.
candidates.explanation: The passage explains how the frog survives freezing (ice outside the cells, glucose and urea inside them), how the ability varies, and why it interests biologists.

A.rationale: The frogs do freeze; they are buried under only a few inches of leaf litter.

C.rationale: The passage says no one yet knows how far the frog's methods can be copied.

D.rationale: Both use the same methods; the Alaskan frogs simply store more glycogen and urea.

hints: What does most of the passage explain?
candidates.remember: A main idea covers what most of the passage explains.

candidates.stem: Based on paragraph 2, a wood frog's cells survive freezing mainly because:

choices.A: the frog's cells contain no water during winter.
choices.B: cold temperatures alone cannot damage animal cells.
choices.C: the frog's body never drops below the freezing point.
choices.D: ice forms around them rather than inside them.

candidates.evidence: Ice builds up in the spaces between its cells
candidates.explanation: Ice crystals inside a cell tear its membrane; the frog keeps ice in the spaces between cells while the water inside stays mostly liquid.

A.rationale: The cells lose some water but keep liquid inside.

B.rationale: The paragraph says ice inside cells is what damages them.

C.rationale: Much of the water in the frog's body turns to ice.

hints: Where does the ice form, and why does that matter?

strategy.explanation: Read the sentence that begins 'The wood frog survives by'.

candidates.remember: Connect a danger to the strategy that avoids it.

candidates.stem: The passage suggests that, compared with a frozen wood frog, a wood frog that has not yet begun to freeze would most likely have:

choices.A: much less glucose in its blood.
choices.B: much less glycogen stored in its liver.
choices.C: a slower heartbeat than a frozen frog has.
choices.D: more ice in the spaces between its cells.

candidates.evidence: Within minutes after ice first touches its skin
candidates.explanation: Glucose release begins only after ice touches the frog's skin, and levels then rise to many times normal; before freezing, blood glucose would be at its normal, much lower level.

B.rationale: Before freezing, the liver still holds its glycogen; it is converted only once ice touches the skin.

C.rationale: A frozen frog's heart has stopped entirely.

D.rationale: A frog that has not begun to freeze has no ice.

hints: When does the glucose release begin?

strategy.explanation: Find the trigger for the glucose release.

candidates.remember: A process that starts at a trigger has not happened before the trigger.

candidates.subskill: Applying a mechanism to explain a difference
candidates.stem: Based on the passage, the Alaskan frogs' larger stores of glycogen most likely help them survive colder temperatures because:

choices.A: glycogen itself freezes at a lower temperature than water does.
choices.B: larger glycogen stores keep ice from forming outside the cells.
choices.C: the liver can turn more glycogen into glucose when freezing begins.
choices.D: glycogen lets the frog's heart keep beating while it is frozen.

candidates.evidence: the frog's liver begins converting a stored carbohydrate called glycogen into the sugar glucose
candidates.explanation: Paragraph 3 explains that glycogen is the source of the protective glucose. Frogs with more glycogen can produce more glucose, protecting their cells at lower temperatures.

A.rationale: The passage says glycogen is converted to glucose; it says nothing about glycogen's freezing point.

B.rationale: Ice still forms outside the cells; that is part of the frog's strategy.

D.rationale: The heart stops in all frozen wood frogs.

hints: What does glycogen become, and what does that do?
candidates.remember: Use a mechanism explained earlier to account for a later finding.

author_checklist.hardness: Students must link paragraph 4's finding to paragraph 3's mechanism; the 'glycogen freezes lower' choice invents a property.

candidates.subskill: Meaning of a word in context
candidates.stem: As it is used in paragraph 2, the word "concentrated" most nearly means:
candidates.evidence: the fluid left inside becomes more concentrated and harder to freeze
candidates.explanation: As cells lose water, the substances in the remaining fluid are dissolved in less water, so the fluid is less diluted, which makes it harder to freeze.

A.rationale: This is a familiar meaning for attention, but the passage describes a fluid.

C.rationale: The fluid stays inside each cell; the point is that less water dilutes it.

D.rationale: Nothing in the passage concerns exercise.

hints: What happens to the fluid when water leaves the cell?

strategy.explanation: Predict a word for 'with less water mixed in.'

candidates.remember: Scientific uses of familiar words often have a precise technical meaning.

candidates.stem: The author mentions that the frog's glucose levels would be "deadly to a human" (paragraph 3) mainly to:

choices.A: warn readers about the dangers of high blood sugar.
choices.B: suggest that frogs and humans have identical blood chemistry.
choices.C: emphasize how extreme the frog's rise in blood sugar is.
choices.D: explain why the frog's heart stops when it freezes.

candidates.evidence: high enough to be deadly to a human
candidates.explanation: Comparing the level to what would kill a human gives readers a sense of how far beyond normal the frog's blood sugar goes.

A.rationale: The passage is not giving health advice.

B.rationale: The comparison stresses a difference, not a similarity.

D.rationale: The heart stops because of freezing, not because of glucose.

hints: What does the comparison tell readers about the frog's glucose?
candidates.remember: Comparisons to familiar cases help readers grasp an extreme.

candidates.stem: Which of the following findings, if true, would most directly support the passage's claim that glucose protects the frog's cells during freezing?

choices.A: Frogs with more glucose in their blood hopped faster after thawing in spring.
choices.B: Frogs in Alaska stored more urea in the fall than southern frogs did.
choices.C: Frogs began releasing glucose a few minutes after ice touched their skin.
choices.D: Frogs kept from releasing glucose died after freezing that untreated frogs survived.

candidates.evidence: The sugar moves into the cells, where it holds on to water and limits how far the cells shrink.
candidates.explanation: If frogs that cannot release glucose die under the same freezing that others survive, glucose must be doing protective work. The other choices concern timing, urea or behavior after thawing.

A.rationale: Speed after thawing does not show that glucose protected cells during freezing.

C.rationale: This shows when glucose is released, not that it protects the cells.

hints: What experiment would isolate glucose's effect?

strategy.explanation: Ask which finding tests what happens without glucose.

candidates.remember: To show that something protects, show what happens without it.

author_checklist.hardness: Students must choose the finding that isolates glucose's effect; the timing choice is true but does not test protection.

candidates.stem: The last paragraph mainly serves to:

choices.A: explain why the frog's abilities matter beyond the frog itself.
choices.B: describe how human organs are frozen for transplant today.
choices.C: argue that the frog's methods will soon be copied in hospitals.
choices.D: compare the wood frog with other animals that survive freezing.

candidates.evidence: Biologists are interested in the wood frog for more than its own sake.
candidates.explanation: After explaining how the frog survives, the passage ends by connecting it to a human problem, preserving organs for transplant.

B.rationale: The paragraph says organs cannot yet be safely frozen.

C.rationale: The paragraph says no one yet knows how far they can be copied.

hints: What topic does the last paragraph connect the frog to?
candidates.remember: A final paragraph often shows why a topic matters more widely.

candidates.stem: The author describes the frozen frog as being in a state that "looks, by every ordinary sign, like death" (paragraph 1) mainly in order to:

choices.A: suggest that many wood frogs do not survive the winter.
choices.B: set up the surprise that the frog revives each spring.
choices.C: argue that scientists once wrongly believed the frogs were dead.
choices.D: explain why the frog is buried under leaf litter in winter.

candidates.evidence: In spring, it thaws, its heart starts again
candidates.explanation: By stressing that the frozen frog shows every sign of death, the author makes its spring revival, described right after, more striking and sets up the question the passage answers.

A.rationale: The passage presents freezing as something the frog survives, not a common cause of death.

C.rationale: The passage never describes earlier scientists' beliefs.

D.rationale: The description concerns how the frog looks, not where it spends the winter.

hints: What happens right after the description?
candidates.remember: Openings often set up a surprise the rest of the passage explains.

revision_log.reason: Round-1 blind solves (both matched every key) found that R039-02 and R039-09 tested the same fact (ice forms outside, not inside, the cells), so 02's key gave 09 away; both also noted that 'stored starch' is loose for glycogen. Replaced 09 with an item on the opening description ('like death') and changed the passage to 'a stored carbohydrate called glycogen'. Whole batch re-solved blind.
